title: The Source of Distraction is Not What You Think
author: Nir Eyal
summary: Eyal argues that distraction is not a property of any particular activity but a mismatch between what you planned to do and what you actually did. He opens with the observation that attention is a narrow filter, screening out most of what is happening around us, and that the filter is usually doing useful work. The problem is not the filter but the moments when the wrong thing gets through. From there he attacks the common assumption that distraction means phones and social media and that necessary work tasks are safe by definition. Answering email can be the worst kind of distraction precisely because it looks like work and therefore escapes notice. The hinge of the argument is intent: a nap, a YouTube video or a conversation with a colleague is traction if you planned it and distraction if you did not. Eyal reframes the diagnostic question from what is distracting me, which hands responsibility to the phone or the coworker, to what did I plan to do. Only after naming that gap, he says, do you have a problem you can actually work on.
points: Eyal defines distraction relationally rather than categorically: it is the gap between premeditated intent and actual behavior, not a list of bad activities.
He singles out legitimate work tasks such as email as the most dangerous distractions because they pass unnoticed as productivity.
The traction and distraction pairing from Indistractable does the analytic work, letting naps and TikTok count as either depending on the plan.
He rejects the question what is distracting me because it assigns blame to a proximal cause like a phone, a coworker or a child.
The practical move is to audit the mismatch first, on the grounds that you cannot solve a distraction problem until you can name what you were distracted from.
quotes: Modern neuroscience has found that we don't see the world as it is; we see it filtered by our beliefs. We live life through a keyhole.

Just because a task is something you need to do at some point doesn't mean it's not a distraction. In fact, that's the worst kind of distraction because you don't even realize what it's doing to your attention.
Remember: You can't say you got distracted unless you know what you got distracted from.
Traction is any action that pulls us toward what we said we'd do, while distraction pulls us away.
Many things we think are distractions are perfectly worthwhile activities at the right time.

Meanwhile, many things that look "productive" can pull us off course. I can spend an hour answering work messages and still avoid the one task I had previously decided was important, like doing my taxes or editing a blog post.
The activity itself doesn't tell us much. We have to check it against our premeditated intention.
Then, see if there's a mismatch between what you said you would give your attention to (traction) and what you did instead (distraction).
